newsitem.title: UK: Mark mostly firm on Eurocrosses, rates in focus.
newsitem.headline: Mark mostly firm on Eurocrosses, rates in focus.

text.p: The German mark was mostly firmer on its European cross rates in Europe amid German interest rate jitters which also steered dollar/mark lower, said traders.

Traders said the mark should remain supported ahead of the German securities repurchase tender on Tuesday, with some expecting the central bank to announce a variable rate repo. The Bundesbank holds its regular council meeting on Thursday after a four-week summer recess.
Aside from dollar/mark stumble and German interest rate concerns, attention is also focused on global asset markets after a steep slide in U.S. stocks Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average of leading U.S. stocks posted its second-biggest point loss on Friday, shaken partly by an earnings warning from consumer products giant Gillette Co.
"The key factor is the Dow. If it continues to come off this afternoon the dollar could continue under pressure and the mark/crosses could see some more buying," said a trader at a Finnish bank.
Germany's IBIS Dax Index rose back above 4,000 points in pre-bourse computer dealings after stumbling sharply lower in early trade.
Against the Nordic currencies, the mark was mostly firm.
Barring, however, a stumble against the Finnish markka. At 0940 GMT, mark/markka was at 2.9940/70, down from an earlier high of 3.0000 and against 2.9960/90 in late Europe.
Traders said the mark was softer after its jump against the markka last week.
"Mark/Finny is seeing some natural sellers...But there is not much business going through and the market is thin. After the fall on Friday, people are wary," said the dealer.
But the mark pushed up against the Norwegian and Swedish crowns, rising to a five-week high of 4.1720 and a peak of 4.3890 -- its highest since July 11 -- respectively.
At 0945 GMT, mark/Norwegian crown stood at 4.1655/85 against 4.1665/95 in late Europe on Friday. Mark/Swedish crown was at 4.3740/70 against 4.3790/20.
Against the Swiss franc the mark stood at 82.85/88 against 82.57/60 in late Europe. Mark/Italian lira was firmer at 977.65/7.85 against 976.40/90 in late Europe.

Aside from rate speculation, traders said the mark was also underpinned after German Chancellor Kohl said in an interview with ZDF TV, released on Sunday, that Europe's planned single currency would be stable. "We don't want a weak euro," Kohl said.
"If the dollar doesn't bounce, we will see the mark strengthening further," said a trader at a European bank.
